杖鼓屬膜鳴樂器，來自韓國傳統音樂，音色由沙漏形鼓身兩面不同皮革產生。左面厚牛皮、: The janggu is a membranophone from Korean traditional music, and its timbre comes from the different skins on the two faces of the hourglass-shaped body. The left face is thick cowhide, horsehide or deerskin and sounds lower; the right face is dogskin or thin horsehide and sounds higher. A wider central tube gives a deep, husky sound, a narrower one a hard, brittle sound. It is played by striking the large face with the left hand and the small face with a bamboo stick in the right, or with two sticks at once, and can produce a drum stroke, a stick stroke, the two together, or a shaken stroke; volume is then controlled by the hand and the stick, by changes of speed and force. Beside the smaller hourglass drum of the same family, the yogo, the janggu has a larger body, and its two faces differ in pitch and timbre, which in ensemble is seen as the union of yin and yang.
杖鼓屬膜鳴樂器，最早圖像見於新羅時期鐘銘與高句麗墓壁畫；文字記錄可追溯高麗文宗時: The janggu is a membranophone, and its earliest images appear on Silla-period bell inscriptions and in Goguryeo tomb murals; written records go back to the reign of King Munjong of Goryeo, the Goryeo-sa of 1451 records the gifts at a banquet of Emperor Huizong of Song in 1114 and the word "janggu", and by 1076 there was a title for its players. Its form may have developed from the smaller hourglass drum yogo, which came from the Indian idakka during the Silla period; in the Goryeo period it grew to today's size, and the Akhak gwebeom describes a lacquered-cloth shell, a horsehide head and the left- and right-hand ways of playing.
杖鼓常見於韓國傳統音樂，包括宮廷音樂、吹管音樂、民間音樂與巫俗音樂，也用於聲樂、: The janggu is common in Korean traditional music, including court music, wind music, folk music and shamanic music, and it is also used for song, dance and theatre. In samul nori it plays with the buk, the jing and the kkwaenggwari; pungmul players beat it for folk songs and in shamanic rites. Traditionally the right hand strikes the high face with a bamboo stick (yeolchae) and the left hand beats the low face with the palm; today a beater (gungchae) and the bamboo stick are often used together. It can be set on the floor to play sanjo, or hung from the shoulder to be played while moving, and it appears in both dangak and hyangak.
杖鼓琴身為沙漏形，兩面蒙皮，以金屬箍與繩索固定。左面用厚牛皮、馬皮或鹿皮，右面用: The body of the janggu is hourglass-shaped, with skins on both faces held by metal hoops and rope. The left face uses thick cowhide, horsehide or deerskin and the right face dogskin or a lighter horsehide. The Akhak gwebeom records that a shell of waist-wood or lacquered cloth is best, porcelain next and tile poor, that the lacquer is black or vermilion, that each face has an iron hoop, the large face a white raw horsehide and the small face a raw horsehide. The beaters include those with a bamboo-root handle and a hardwood or deer-horn head, and there are plastic beaters for beginners; another kind is made entirely of bamboo.

Players usually beat the low face with the bare hand and strike the high face with a bamboo stick, and two sticks together are also common today; the drum can be set on the floor or hung from the shoulder. It is used in court music, wind music, folk music, shamanic music, song, dance and the traditional performing arts, and it is one of the four instruments of samul nori.
演奏杖鼓時，可將鼓置於地面，或以肩帶懸掛於身上；懸掛方式因人、地區與演奏者喜好而: To play the janggu you can set the drum on the floor or hang it on the body with a shoulder strap; how it is hung varies with the player, the region and personal taste. Traditionally the right hand strikes the high face on the right with a thin bamboo stick (yeolchae) and the left hand beats the low face on the left with the bare hand; today the beater (gungchae) and the thin stick are often used together. A beginner can first tell the two faces apart, then practise the basic spoken sounds: the thin stick gives "tta", the beater gives "gung", and striking both faces together gives "deong". The player can also vary speed, force and timbre with hand and stick, moving the shoulder with the rhythm.
